content: Electrochemistry studies chemical reactions that produce or consume electricity. In fruit batteries, chemical energy converts to electrical energy through redox (reduction-oxidation) reactions. The fruit's acidic juice acts as an electrolyte, containing ions that can carry electric current. When two different metals (electrodes) are inserted into the fruit, they have different tendencies to lose electrons (different reduction potentials). The more reactive metal (typically zinc) oxidizes, losing electrons: Zn â ZnÂ²âº + 2eâ». These electrons flow through an external circuit to the less reactive metal (typically copper), where they reduce hydrogen ions from the acid: 2Hâº + 2eâ» â Hâ. This creates an electric potential difference (voltage) between the electrodes, driving current through the circuit. The maximum voltage of a single fruit cell is determined by the difference in reduction potentials of the electrode materials, typically 0.5-1.0 volts. Connecting multiple fruit cells in series adds their voltages, potentially providing enough potential difference to light an LED (typically requiring 1.5-3.0 volts). The internal resistance of fruit batteries is relatively high, limiting current flow and making them inefficient power sources for high-energy applications.

scenario.title: Fruit Power Laboratory
scenario.content: Students create virtual fruit batteries to power LED circuits, experimenting with different fruits, electrodes, and circuit configurations. The simulation visualizes ion movement within the electrolyte and electron flow through the external circuit, highlighting the redox reactions occurring at each electrode. Students can measure voltage, current, and power output while manipulating variables like fruit acidity, electrode materials, electrode surface area, and temperature. The simulation demonstrates how connecting batteries in series increases voltage while parallel connections increase current capacity. Interactive elements allow students to build increasingly complex circuits with LEDs of different colors (requiring different voltages) and other components. Challenge modes ask students to design optimal battery configurations for specific power requirements, teaching practical applications of electrochemical principles.

hypothesis.description: Students will construct functioning electrochemical cells by applying redox principles to convert chemical energy to electrical energy. They will predict how variations in materials and configurations affect cell performance, and design optimal setups for specific voltage and current requirements.
